task.title: Intermittent Connectivity
task.shortdesc: Identify and correct conditions that cause a client device to lose and restore its network connection repeatedly.

prereq.p: Before you troubleshoot an intermittent connection, make sure that:

ul.li: The or Optical Network Terminal (ONT) is connected to the ISP service.
The affected client device is connected through Ethernet or Wi-Fi.
You know whether the problem affects the local network, Internet access, or both.
You have recorded recent changes to the network, client device, or physical environment.

prereq.note: Make one change at a time. Monitor the connection after each change.

context.p: An intermittent connection stops and starts without a planned disconnection. The problem can affect one client device, multiple devices, or the complete network.
Common causes include a weak Wi-Fi signal, wireless interference, damaged cables, high network activity, unstable power, outdated firmware, or incorrect network settings.
context.note: Record when and where the connection stops. This information can help you identify a device, location, or activity that causes the problem.
Record timestamps affected traffic paths, connection events, channel changes, address assignments, and access-point transitions before you change the configuration.

step.cmd: Identify the affected connection type.

choices.choice: For a wireless connection, confirm that the affected device connects to .
For a wired connection, confirm that the affected device uses a working Ethernet connection.

info.p: Determine whether the problem affects wired devices, wireless devices, or both.

step.cmd: Determine the scope of the problem.

substep.cmd: Test the connection on another client device.
Test one wired device and one wireless device if both connection types are available.
Record which devices lose their connections.

ul.li: If only one device is affected, check the client device and its network settings.
If only wireless devices are affected, check the Wi-Fi signal, interference, band, and wireless configuration.
If only wired devices are affected, check the Ethernet cables, ports, and Ethernet switch.
If all devices are affected, check the router, modem or ONT, power supply, and ISP service.

step.stepresult: The affected devices and connection types are identified.

step.cmd: Record when the connection stops.

info.p: Record the following information:

ul.li: The date and time of each disconnection
The application or activity in use
Whether the connection returns without user action

info.note: Look for a repeated pattern. For example, the problem can occur in one room or when an appliance operates.

step.cmd: Check the ISP service status.

info.p: Check whether the ISP has reported a service interruption or maintenance activity.
If all devices lose Internet access but remain connected to the local network, the ISP service or WAN connection can be the cause.

step.cmd: Check whether the affected device can access the during the problem.

substep.cmd: Open a supported web browser.
Go to .
Confirm whether the sign-in page for the opens.

ul.li: If the sign-in page opens, the local network is available. Check the WAN and ISP connection.
If the sign-in page does not open, check the local wired or wireless connection.

step.cmd: Check the status indicators on the or ONT and the .

info.p: Check whether the power, service, WAN, LAN, or Wi-Fi indicators change when the connection stops.
info.note: Indicator names, colors, and patterns can differ by device. Refer to the instructions supplied with the device.

step.cmd: Check the power connections.

substep.cmd: Make sure that each power adapter is fully connected.
Check each power cable and adapter for visible damage.
Connect the network equipment to a reliable electrical outlet.
Confirm that the router does not restart when the connection stops.

info.note: Do not use a damaged or incompatible power adapter. Use only an adapter approved for the device.

step.cmd: Check the network cables and ports.

substep.cmd: Make sure that the Ethernet cable from the modem or ONT is fully connected to the on the router.
Make sure that each wired client device is connected to an available LAN port.
Check each Ethernet cable for loose connectors or visible damage.
Replace a suspected cable with a known working cable.
Connect the cable to another compatible port if one is available.

step.stepresult: The network devices have stable physical connections.

step.cmd: Check the Wi-Fi signal on the affected device.

substep.cmd: Move the affected device closer to the .
Monitor the connection in the new location.

info.p: If the connection becomes stable near the router, distance or physical obstructions can be the cause.
For more information, see .

step.cmd: Check the router location.

info.p: Make sure that the router is:

ul.li: Near the center of the required coverage area
On an open and elevated surface
Outside a closed cabinet or drawer
Away from sources of wireless interference

info.p: For more information, see .

step.cmd: Check for wireless interference.

info.p: Monitor the connection when nearby wireless equipment and household appliances are active.
Increase the distance between the router and potential sources of interference, such as:
For more information, see .

step.stepresult: The test determines whether interference contributes to the connection problem.

step.cmd: Test the affected device on another Wi-Fi band.

choices.choice: Use the 2.4 GHz band when the device is far from the router or behind several physical obstructions.
Use the 5 GHz band when the compatible device is near the router.

info.p: Monitor the connection on each supported band. Use the band that provides the more stable connection.
For more information, see .

step.cmd: Remove the saved Wi-Fi network from the affected device and reconnect it.

substep.cmd: Open the Wi-Fi settings on the device.
Select .
Select the option to forget or remove the network.
Select again.
Enter the current .
Monitor the connection.

info.note: Make sure that you know the current Wi-Fi password before you remove the saved network.

step.cmd: Review the power-saving settings on the affected client device.

info.p: Disable the setting that turns off the Wi-Fi adapter to save power if the connection stops when the device is inactive.
info.note: Control names and available settings depend on the client device and operating system.
Changing a power-saving setting can increase battery use.

step.cmd: Check for high network activity.

info.p: Open the and review theconnected devices.
Look for activities such as:
Stop unnecessary network activity and monitor the connection again.

step.cmd: Check the access point or mesh connection.

info.p: If the affected device connects through the or , confirm that the wireless coverage point has a reliable network connection.
Move a wireless mesh node closer to the main router or another connected node if the backhaul connection is weak.
For more information, see .
info.note: Do not put a mesh node in an area where the existing Wi-Fi signal is unusable.

step.cmd: Restart the affected client device.

info.p: Reconnect the device to and monitor the connection.

step.cmd: Restart the network devices if multiple devices are affected.

substep.cmd: Turn off the client devices.
Turn off the .
Turn off the or ONT if the ISP permits this action.
Wait until the devices turn off completely.
Turn on the or ONT.
Wait until the Internet service indicator shows normal operation.
Turn on the .
Wait until the router indicators show normal operation.
Turn on the client devices.

info.note: Do not press the reset button. A factory reset can remove the custom network configuration.

step.cmd: Check for an approved firmware update for the .

info.p: Use the update function in the or get approved firmware from the .
info.note: Do not turn off the router during a firmware update.
Install only firmware intended for and the applicable .

step.cmd: Update the affected client device.

info.p: Install approved operating-system, Wi-Fi adapter, and device firmware updates.
Restart the client device if the update process requires a restart.

step.cmd: Verify the client network configuration.

substep.cmd: Confirm that the client device has a valid address.
Confirm that the default gateway is .
Confirm that the subnet mask is .
Confirm that a valid DNS server is assigned.

info.p: If the device uses automatic configuration, confirm that the assigns an address from .
info.note: The network settings can differ if an administrator changed the default network configuration.

step.cmd: Renew the client DHCP configuration.

info.p: Disconnect and reconnect the network interface, or use the operating-system function that renews the DHCP configuration.
Check the router event information for repeated address assignment failures or duplicate-address messages.

step.cmd: Review wireless channel behavior.

info.p: Check whether the router, access point, or mesh system changes channels when the connection stops.
Review channel utilization and nearby wireless networks. Keep automatic channel selection enabled when wireless conditions change frequently.
info.note: If you manually select , confirm that the channel is permitted and suitable for the local wireless environment.

step.cmd: Review access-point and mesh roaming behavior.

info.p: Confirm which access point or mesh node serves the client device before and after each disconnection.
Check for inconsistent SSIDs, security modes, or encryption settings across wireless coverage points.
Review coverage overlap and transmit-power settings if the problem occurs when the device moves between coverage areas.

step.cmd: Review available network event logs.

info.p: Compare the event times with the recorded disconnections. Look for:
info.note: Do not share logs that contain passwords, access tokens, private keys, or other confidential information.

step.cmd: Monitor the connection under normal use conditions.

substep.cmd: Put the client device in its normal use location.
Connect the device to .
Use the applications that were active when the problem occurred.
Confirm that the local network and Internet connections remain available.

info.note: Record connection uptime, signal strength, channel, connected access point, latency, and packet loss during the monitoring period.

step.stepresult: The client device maintains a stable network connection.

result.p: The affected client devices maintain stable access to the local network and Internet services.

postreq.p: If the connection continues to stop and start, collect the following information:

ul.li: The affected devices and connection types
The date and time of each disconnection
The locations where the problem occurs
The connected access point or mesh node
Relevant event logs, channel information, signal measurements, DHCP events, latency, and packet-loss results

postreq.note: Do not send Wi-Fi passwords, administrator passwords, account passwords, access tokens, or other confidential credentials to technical support.
